passage:
At every family function, someone would say, "Kashish is the shy one," before I'd even opened my mouth. After a while I stopped trying. If everyone already knew I was shy, what was the point? Then Shalini Ma'am came to teach us in Class 5. She never called me shy, not once. When I read one line aloud in a tiny voice, she said, "You read that line in front of thirty people. That was brave." The next week I read two lines. At Diwali, when Chachi said, "Oh, our shy Kashish," I heard myself say, "I read two lines in class this week." Chachi blinked. I don't think I'm "the shy one" anymore. I'm someone who gets braver in small steps.
Kashish

qa.q: What did Shalini Ma'am say after Kashish read one line?
qa.a: "You read that line in front of thirty people. That was brave."

qa.q: Why did Kashish stop trying at family functions?
qa.a: Kashish had come to believe being shy was fixed, so trying felt pointless.

qa.q: What did Shalini Ma'am do instead of labelling, and what changed?
qa.a: She praised the small brave step, and the next week Kashish read two lines.

qa.q: How might Chachi feel when Kashish answers with the two lines?
qa.a: She seemed surprised, blinking, and may start to see Kashish differently.

grounding: A child labelled shy by relatives starts to believe it, until a teacher praises small brave steps instead.

passage:
Note for Sunaina's parents, from Kavitha, class teacher
When I asked Sunaina to take the register to the office today, she said, "I can't, I'm shy. Everyone says so." She is eight, and she already believes it is who she is. At the parents' evening I noticed she was introduced to me the same way. I'd like to suggest we stop using the word, at school and at home. Instead, let's notice small brave steps. Today she carried the register with a friend and said "good morning" to the office staff in a whisper. I told her, "You did something new today." She smiled all through lunch. Tomorrow she will try it on her own.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say when asked to take the register?
qa.a: "I can't, I'm shy. Everyone says so."

qa.q: What does Sunaina's reply show she believes about herself?
qa.a: She believes shyness is who she is, not something that can change.

qa.q: What change does Kavitha suggest to Sunaina's parents?
qa.a: To stop using the word "shy" and to notice small brave steps instead.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel after hearing "You did something new today"?
qa.a: She felt proud and capable; she smiled all through lunch.

grounding: A teacher sees an eight-year-old who has taken on the shy label and asks her parents to drop it and praise small brave steps.

passage:
Friday
Everyone says I'm shy. Mummy says it when aunties visit: 'He's the shy one.' Dadi says it. Even my cousin says it. So I stay quiet, because that's what shy people do. Today in science Bhavna Ma'am asked why the ice melted faster in the steel bowl. I knew. My heart was going fast, but I put my hand up halfway, and she saw. I said it very softly. She didn't say, 'Oh, our shy boy spoke!' like Mrs. Iyer did last year. She said, 'That was a brave thing, putting your hand up. And a good answer.' I've been thinking about 'brave' all evening. Nobody has called me that before. Maybe I'm not the shy one. Maybe I'm someone who can do brave things.
Darshan

qa.q: What question did Bhavna Ma'am ask in science?
qa.a: Why the ice melted faster in the steel bowl.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel on being called brave?
qa.a: He felt surprised and quietly proud, thinking about the word all evening.

qa.q: What did Bhavna Ma'am do differently from Mrs. Iyer?
qa.a: She avoided the 'shy' label and praised the brave step of raising his hand, so he felt capable rather than defective.

qa.q: What might the aunties think when Mummy says 'He's the shy one'?
qa.a: They probably accept it as a fact about Darshan, not realising the label is shaping how he sees himself.

grounding: Shows a child who has started to believe the 'shy' label everyone gives him, and a teacher who praises a small brave step instead.

passage: In the village near Karnal, everyone had decided Payal was shy. 'She won't talk,' her Dadi told visitors. 'Don't expect anything from her.' So Payal didn't talk. When her Chacha Akash came home from the city for Lohri, he noticed she stood behind the door whenever guests came. He didn't call her shy. On the second evening he handed her a ten-rupee note. 'Can you buy me some rewri from Ramlal's shop?' Payal's stomach flipped. She went, stood at the counter a long time, and finally said, 'Rewri, please.' When she came back, Akash Chacha grinned. 'You asked him yourself? That took guts.' That night, when guests came for the bonfire, Payal stood by the door again, but in front of it this time.

qa.q: What did Akash Chacha ask Payal to buy?
qa.a: Some rewri from Ramlal's shop.

qa.q: What did Payal feel when handed the note?
qa.a: Her stomach flipped; she felt nervous about speaking to the shopkeeper.

qa.q: How did Akash Chacha help without labelling Payal?
qa.a: He gave her a small brave task and praised her for it, so she saw herself as capable rather than 'shy'.

qa.q: How might Dadi's words to visitors affect Payal?
qa.a: Hearing 'She won't talk' again and again made Payal believe it, so she stayed silent.

grounding: Shows a child who has come to believe she is 'the shy one', and an adult who avoids the label and praises a small brave step.

passage: At Leila's school in Lisbon, the report cards had said the same thing for three years: 'Leila is very shy.' Leila had read them. Now, in class games, she stood at the back, because that's where the shy girl stood. Her new teacher, Senhor Paulo, never used the word. On Tuesday he noticed she had read a whole page aloud to her partner in pair reading, quietly but without stopping. At the end of the lesson he knelt by her desk. 'You read that whole page to Inês. That was a brave step.' Leila looked at her shoes, but her mouth twitched. On Thursday, when he asked for a volunteer to hand out books, her hand went up, just to her shoulder. He saw it. 'Leila, thank you.'

qa.q: What had the report cards said for three years?
qa.a: 'Leila is very shy.'

qa.q: What does Leila's mouth twitching suggest?
qa.a: She felt pleased and a little proud, even while looking at her shoes.

qa.q: Why did Senhor Paulo's praise work?
qa.a: He named a specific brave step instead of the label, so Leila felt capable and tried another small step on Thursday.

qa.q: How might Inês have experienced Leila's reading?
qa.a: Inês heard Leila read a whole page, and may have seen her as a steady partner rather than 'the shy girl'.

grounding: Shows a child who has come to see herself through the 'shy' label, and a teacher who avoids it and praises small brave steps.

passage:
"This is Devika, she's our shy one," her mother told the new art teacher on the first day. Devika had heard it at every family function, at the tailor's, at the bus stop. Lately she'd started saying it herself: "I can't, I'm shy."
The teacher, Ganga Ma'am, only smiled and said, "Hello, Devika."
In class, Ganga Ma'am asked who would pass out the paints. Devika didn't raise her hand, but she stood up when asked. "Thank you, that was helpful."
The next week, Devika showed her painting to the table next to her. Ganga Ma'am noticed. "You shared your work. That took some courage."
At the end of term, Devika raised her hand to explain her own collage. Her voice wobbled, but she finished.

qa.q: What did Devika's mother call her on the first day?
qa.a: She called her "our shy one".

qa.q: How did Devika feel about herself before art class changed things?
qa.a: She felt stuck and small, believing shyness was who she was; she even said, "I can't, I'm shy."

qa.q: Which of Ganga Ma'am's choices helped Devika, and why?
qa.a: Ganga Ma'am never used the shy label and praised each small brave step, like handing out paints and sharing work, so Devika began to feel capable.

qa.q: How might Devika's mother see her differently after the term?
qa.a: Seeing Devika explain her own collage, her mother might notice she can speak up in her own time, not just "our shy one".

grounding: Shows a child who has come to believe the shy label and a teacher who avoids it and praises small brave steps instead.
